1:
Which Persian king is meant is settled by all who raise it, and by the same kind of argument. Gill rejects both the Mede and the later Darius whom some scholars had proposed, on the ground that the later date would require the governor and the high priest to hold office a hundred and thirty-eight years and some exiles to have lived beyond two hundred; he settles on the son of Hystaspes. Ellicott calls the later identification absurd and disposes of it in one stroke, that men were still living who had seen the first temple. Calvin reaches the same king by counting the reigns, and dismisses the rabbinic notion that he was the son of Ahasuerus by Esther as a bold fancy hazarded in a matter unknown. On the governor's parentage Ellicott and Wesley agree against the surface of the text, that he was strictly the son of Pedaiah, who had contracted a levirate marriage with his brother's widow, so that the sonship named here is adoptive. Clarke presses the political limit instead: none of their own governors was absolute, the Persians allowing them their own laws but treating them as a colony under the satrap beyond the river.

On the prophet himself the voices differ in what they will admit. Keil and Delitzsch confine themselves to what the headings yield, that the name means the festal one and that he began under this king, and dismiss the extra-biblical reports, that he came from Babylon while young and was buried near the priests, as having no evidence at all. Clarke states the same biography as probable fact, that he was born in Babylon during the captivity and was the first prophet sent after the return, and fills in the history around it, the first edict revoked through evil advice, the prohibition renewed by the next king, the permission restored by this one. Ellicott makes the date itself significant, the first day being the new moon, a holy day marked by suspension of labour and special services and therefore a fitting occasion, with the added custom that people resorted to the prophets for instruction on such days; and the phrase by the hand of Haggai marks the Lord as the direct source and the prophet only as the vehicle. Henry sets the moment in the history of prophecy itself, the lamp of the older prophecy making some bright efforts before it expires, after a long stretch with no open vision.

The excuse that the time had not come is taken apart in four ways. Clarke supposes they miscounted the seventy years, and reports the calculation showing that sixty-nine had been completed from the last siege. Calvin turns the same chronology against them: had the term truly been unfinished the excuse would have been ready to hand, and its absence proves the delay was indifference; he then reconstructs the pretexts they must have used, that their earlier haste had been punished, that their fathers had lived many ages without a temple, and that an altar and sacrifices would serve while each man built his own house. Ellicott renders it that it is not yet time to come, that is, to assemble and begin preparations, and guesses their unstated ground to be a pretended dread of Persian hostility. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the grammar, hearing contempt in the phrase this people, taking the negative as meaning not yet, distinguishing coming to the house from building it, and rejecting a proposed alteration of the text as unnecessary. Gill notes only that the title of hosts is prefixed to show the words were not the prophet's. Henry supplies the moral the others leave implicit, that many a good work is put by simply by being put off, and that it is bad to neglect a duty but worse to plead providence in patronage of the neglect.
3:
The repetition of the opening formula is read as structure by two voices. Gill takes it to mark a second and distinct prophecy, the first delivered to the two governors and left with them to weigh, this one sent to the people themselves. Keil and Delitzsch make it rhetorical rather than administrative, the formula repeated so that the word of the Lord stands out sharply against the speech of the people it answers. On the panelled houses they add the grammar: the opening particle is interrogative and not the article, the pronoun is strengthened, and the word for panelled stands in apposition, meaning walls covered or inlaid with costly woodwork, so that to live in such a house was a mark of luxury. Gill says the same in plainer terms, that men who could find time to line their houses with cedar, and sit in them in ease and sloth, could hardly plead that no time had come. Ellicott calls the question a crushing retort and sharpens it against their own excuse: if the adverse decree had not stopped them raising magnificent residences, it could not reasonably excuse an utter neglect of the other house. Clarke supplies the interval that makes the reproach bite, a foundation laid fourteen years before and some considerable progress made, lying waste ever since.

The summons to consider is treated as a formula with a method behind it. Keil and Delitzsch note that setting the heart upon one's ways is a favourite phrase of this prophet and gloss it as attending to designs, actions and their consequences. Ellicott points out the order of the argument, that the results are set out first and the people left to infer from them what their conduct has been. Calvin explains why the prophet proceeds so: the teachable need only a word, but those perversely addicted to their sins must be more sharply urged, and so he puts their own punishments before them, on the principle that experience is the teacher of fools. He presses it into speech: if the authority of God weighs nothing with you, at least consider how he deals with you, and let these judgments induce you to repent. What remains, when instruction and warning have failed, is that they be drawn by force while they are chastised.

The catalogue of frustrated labour divides on tense and on what the curse actually is. Calvin insists it is past and not future, since the call to apply the heart to their ways would be pointless if only a coming punishment were denounced; and he distinguishes two ways God punishes, by withholding the produce so that the heavens and earth are dry, or by taking the nourishing power out of what is produced, so that bread and wine give no support and men eat without being satisfied. He finds both here, and adds the vanishing of money laid up as the most manifest proof of wrath, remarking that the disputed words are participles rather than infinitives. Ellicott takes the description more soberly, as implying only that despite all their labour there was not much to eat, drink or put on, and reads the pierced bag as a bold metaphor for the general prevalence of poverty, scarcity raising prices so that money ran away as fast as it was earned. Gill notes the reversal of the ordinary case, much land tilled and much seed sown and a thin crop gathered. Clarke observes that the verse is a string of proverbs, no fewer than five in a few lines, and states the condition flatly, that no labour of their hands will be blessed until the house is rebuilt. Wesley glosses each clause to the same end, that the food does not nourish, the drink does not revive, the clothing gives no comfort, and the earner loses all his labour.
7:
The repeated summons to consider is where Calvin builds his most careful point. He treats the two occurrences as marking two stages of repentance rather than mere emphasis: the first bids them trace the famine and the fruitless labour to God's anger, so that their sin becomes displeasing to them; the second requires the further step, that the sloth which provoked the anger be changed into strenuous activity, since a feeling of displeasure at sin that goes no further is evanescent. He also answers the question the passage raises against itself, why so much weight should rest on a building: the temple was of no great importance in itself, but by it the people were kept in hope and taught to worship spiritually under external symbols, so that neglect of even the outward fabric showed that no zeal for religion remained. He is careful to add the converse, that the same people were often more assiduous in external worship than was needed, and that God scorned the assiduity when the inward feeling was absent. Gill says only that the exhortation is repeated to impress it and to mark its necessity.

Which mountain they are sent to divides the commentators evenly. Gill offers a choice between the northern range, for cedar to be cut and brought, and the temple hill itself, where the timber fetched from the north would be carried. Clarke names the northern range without hesitation and recalls that in the second year of the return cedars had already been procured from there and brought to the coast, and masons and carpenters hired from the Phoenician cities, all of which the long suspension had nearly wasted. Ellicott denies that any one mountain is thought of, taking the term for the high lands generally, as the place where suitable building timber grows. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by a different route, that the article is generic rather than definite, and reject both the temple mountain and the northern range as proposed identifications; fetching wood, they add, is a particularising way of saying provide materials. Wesley passes over the geography and glosses the promise instead, that to take pleasure is to accept their offerings and hear their prayers, and to be glorified is to show his majesty and account himself glorified by them.

On the disappointed expectation the readings differ in where they locate the loss. Gill puts it in the harvest and in trade together, a promising crop that came to little, and expectations of raising a family fortune by vineyards and olives and merchandise that dwindled to nothing, riches diminished instead of increased. Clarke turns the clause against their conduct rather than their crops, that they made great pretensions at first and did a little in the beginning, but so scantily and unwillingly that it had to be rejected. Ellicott keeps to the words, rendering the opening as a turning about for much, and explains the blowing as done for the purpose of dispersing, so that even the little brought into the garner was reduced by continued disfavour. Calvin makes the psychological observation the others do not: a man content with a slender portion is not troubled by scarcity, and those hardened to endure evils do not seek much, so that the sting here falls on people whose desire had led them to seek abundance and grasp at things on every side. He reads the bringing home as the laying up of stores by men who thought that with full storehouses and well-filled bags they had no more to do with God, and takes the blowing for a scorching wind that withers what it touches. Wesley compresses the whole to two glosses, that it answered not the expectation and that God blasted it.
10:
The little word rendered over you is worked at by three voices and comes out the same way in each. Gill would put a stop after it and offers three constructions, that the withholding falls upon them and upon them only and not upon the surrounding nations, or that the sense is that God is against them, or, with the Syriac and the Targum behind him, that it means for your sake. Ellicott settles on the last without canvassing the others, rendering it on your account and referring the cause back to the neglect just named. Calvin agrees on the sense and adds the complaint that one rendering he has before him has passed the word over altogether. Keil and Delitzsch build the same force into their rendering, that the heaven withheld its dew on your account so that no dew fell, and that the earth withheld her produce.

Calvin uses the drought to state the principle that governs his whole reading of the chapter. God did not regard the external and visible building but the end for which it was designed, since sacrifices were never commanded for his own sake but so that by such services true religion might be fostered; the fabric is to be regarded as a pattern of heavenly things, and the neglect of it is reproved because it showed that no care for worship remained. He then observes how the prophets worked: the curses of the law are stated generally, and the prophets took them thence and accommodated them to the case before them, so that this withholding is nothing new but the fulfilment of what had been threatened long before. From that he draws a rule for teachers, that since men in war or famine or pestilence do not of themselves regard the general truth, it must be applied to them as circumstances require, and they must be reminded that God proves by facts what he has testified in his word.

The calling of the drought draws two philological notes and one physical one. Gill hears an elegant play on words that shows the justice of the proceeding by the law of retaliation: they suffered the house of God to lie waste, and therefore he calls for a wasting drought upon their land. He also presses the word called, since every creature obeys when God calls. Ellicott would render it that he invoked a desolation, and points to the parallel where a prophet announces that the Lord has called a famine which will come upon the land for seven years. Clarke says only what the following verse shows, that a drought had been sent which threatened them with scarcity and famine. Wesley notices the last item in the list, that the visitation reached men themselves: their very blood and constitutions were changed, and many diseases afflicted them.
12:
That the leaders are named before the people is treated as significant by everyone who notices it. Gill supposes the governor and the high priest were the first to declare their sense of the former neglect, which set an example that told upon the rest. Calvin makes the same point a general rule about how a message works: when a word is addressed indiscriminately to all, men wait for one another, and nothing moves until those dominant in power and in authority extend a hand; from which he concludes that the more a man excels in honour, the more promptly he ought to undertake what God proposes. Henry presses the humility rather than the influence, that a governor eminently useful in his day did not plead his former merits against a reproof for present remissness, and that a high priest whose own business was to teach was willing to be taught. Clarke states the whole result in a sentence, that when the authority of God is acknowledged his words will be carefully obeyed. On the phrase describing the people, Ellicott leaves the question open, since the word may mean either those restored from exile or merely the remainder; Calvin takes it as the small portion who returned compared with the great number who never availed themselves of the liberty allowed them; and Keil and Delitzsch rule out the reading that would make it the rest of the nation besides the two men named.

Calvin turns the roundabout way the obedience is described into a point about ministry. The prophet could have said briefly that his labour bore fruit, and instead says that the people hearkened to the voice of God and to his own words, which Calvin takes as a deliberate confirming of his call at a time when prophecy had long been rare. He then generalises: men are not sent by divine authority to speak so that God himself may be silent, and the church is not ruled by outward preaching as though God had substituted men in his own place and divested himself of his office, but he speaks by their mouth; and the word of God is not to be distinguished from the words of the prophet as though the prophet had added anything of his own. Henry notices instead the effect of scarcity on hearing, that prophecy was a new thing to them and so an extraordinary regard was paid to the one messenger they had, whereas their fathers, who had many prophets, mocked and misused them; when good preaching is scarce it does most good, while manna rained in plenty is loathed as light bread.

The title given to the prophet in the next verse divides them sharply. Gill reports that some render the word angel, and that from this rendering sprang the notion, taken up by some, that he was not a man at all; he insists it respects only the office of one sent as an ambassador. Keil and Delitzsch are blunter, that the meaning is messenger and not angel, and that many in the time of the fathers misunderstood it so. Clarke takes the other side without argument, calling him the angel of Jehovah, and defends the usage by the pastors of the seven churches who are called the angels of those churches. Ellicott stays with the following phrase and would render it in the Lord's message or on the Lord's mission, and Wesley glosses it as speaking in the words of his master to the whole assembly. On the promise itself Keil and Delitzsch describe its function, that the penitent disposition was met with the assurance of help in order to raise disposition into determination and deed, while Clarke simply exclaims at the encouragement, asking what a man may not do when God is his helper.
14:
The stirring of the spirit is taken by all as the necessary supplement to the preaching. Gill describes it as a rousing from sleep and sloth in governors and common people alike, God working in them both to will and to do, giving a mind for the work, a spirit of industry and of courage, and enabling them to shake off the fear of men that had held them; and he ends by insisting that the Lord only could do this. Clarke states the same as a principle of the spiritual life, that it is not enough for the judgment to be enlightened, since the soul must also be invigorated by the Spirit of God before any good work can be effectually done. Wesley leaves the stirring alone and fastens on the title used here, that this is the name by which God delights to be known among the returned captives, and that it was the name best suited to their present state, compassed on all hands with enemies. Keil and Delitzsch give the verse plainly, the spirit of the governor, of the high priest and of all the remnant stirred, and the coming and working at the house.

The dating of the start is where the voices actually differ. Gill has to decide which reckoning of the sixth month is meant, and rejects the one that would put it in the late winter, which some interpreters had chosen precisely because it seemed a proper season to begin building; he answers that no regard is had here to the fitness of the season but only to the order of the Lord, and settles on the month answering to part of August. Clarke measures the interval as a triumph of preaching, that the prophet received his commission on the first day and by the twenty-fourth had so completely succeeded that he had the satisfaction of seeing the whole people heartily engaged, leaving their own houses to build the other; here was a faithful reprover who found obedient ears. On what filled the three weeks the answers differ. Gill passes on the suggestion that they were spent cutting stone and sawing and hewing wood in preparation. Ellicott supposes they were spent collecting timber in the upland region, as the earlier command had directed, and resuming the work of the house. Calvin gives a third answer that is not about materials at all: the delay came because it was no easy thing to persuade them all, so that they might undertake the work with one mind. He is willing to draw the uncomfortable inference, that although their promptitude is commended there was some mixture of weakness in it, since the effect of the teaching did not appear until the twenty-fourth day. He then quarrels with an editorial decision rather than a translation, complaining of the ignorance of whoever began the second chapter at this verse, since the verse specifies the distance between the day he began to exhort and the success he is reporting, and therefore belongs with what precedes it.
